title: The Inherited Mind: Why You Arrive Already Shaped
reflection: Name one automatic loop of yours when it arrives: this is the loop, not the news. Then plant one small, kind groove beside it.

questions.q: What is a saṁskāra, according to Conversation 4.5?
o: A thought, which comes and goes and leaves no mark on the mind at all.
A rule handed down from teachers, which a person follows by free choice.
A rare insight, which comes to a person only in deep meditation here.
An impression worn in until it becomes a self-sustaining loop.
questions.e: A saṁskāra is worn in by repetition or intensity until it sustains itself. It survives years unmaintained, is woken by a cue and not created by one, deepens every time it runs, and coexists with many others. The uninvited morning worry is one spinning up again.
questions.c: A saṁskāra is a groove worn in until it runs itself

questions.q: A woman wakes each day to an uninvited worry, and tells herself, “this is the loop, not the news.” What is she doing, in the terms of Conversation 4.5?
o: Pushing the worry away by force, so that it can no longer return to the mind.
Naming a saṁskāra in the act without fighting it, which is the first of two moves.
Refusing to feel the worry, since feelings that are named are made worse.
Proving that the worry is wrong, so that it has nothing to stand on.
questions.e: Sarah’s practice is to name the morning groove when it arrives, without arguing with it. The second move is to plant a new, truer groove beside it, by repetition and not force: one small, reliable, kind thing every morning, in the same slot.
questions.c: Name the loop without fighting it, then plant a new groove beside it

questions.q: What is the difference between a saṁskāra and a vāsanā in Conversation 4.5?
o: A saṁskāra is good and a vāsanā is bad, which is why the first is kept.
A saṁskāra is one groove that fires; a vāsanā is many coupled that shape a life.
A saṁskāra is conscious and a vāsanā is not, so only the second can be changed.
A saṁskāra belongs to the body and a vāsanā to the mind, and they never meet.
questions.e: When many related grooves couple together they form a vāsanā, a broad standing orientation that colours a whole kind of experience, as a lifetime of resentment can become the lens a person sees through. A saṁskāra fires in a moment; a vāsanā shapes a life.
questions.c: A saṁskāra fires in a moment; a vāsanā shapes a whole life

questions.q: “Saṁskāras are the enemy, and the aim of practice is to remove every one of them.”
questions.e: The grooves are what the filter is made of, which is why you never meet the world unfiltered. They are not bad: a musician’s skill and a kind person’s compassion are grooves too. The question is which grooves serve fit and which feed the drift, and because grooves are made by repetition they can be remade by repetition.
questions.c: Grooves are not the enemy: the question is which serve fit

questions.q: A student asks whether the laboratory and the contemplative accounts of saṁskāras simply contradict each other. What does Conversation 4.5 say?
o: They disagree about what saṁskāras are and do, and about how to work with them all.
They agree on what saṁskāras do, and differ on where they reside and whether they outlast the body.
They agree on everything, and differ only in the words that they use for it.
They are one account, which has been told in two different languages by two people.
questions.e: The laboratory account puts the grooves in tissue, and on it they end with the brain. The contemplative account places them in a subtler memory-field, of which the brain is the screen, and carries them beyond the body. They agree on what saṁskāras do and diverge on where they reside. The practical work is identical either way.
questions.c: The two accounts agree on what grooves do, not on where they live

questions.q: A teacher catches herself reacting automatically to a certain student. Which next step fits Conversation 4.5?
o: Tell herself that her reaction is wrong, and force it to stop at once and for all.
Choose one different response and repeat it, wearing a truer groove beside the old.
Avoid the student, so that the reaction is never given any chance to fire again.
Accept that the reaction is her nature, and make no attempt to change it at all.
questions.e: James’s practice is to catch his own automatic reaction firing once, then choose one different response and repeat it. Repetition is the whole mechanism. He is not erasing the old groove but starting a truer one next to it.
questions.c: Choose one different response and repeat it beside the old groove

questions.q: A patient is burdened by the thought, “I must fix my whole past.” How does Conversation 4.5 help a doctor reframe this?
o: Separate what is ripening, the hand dealt, and the one move that is hers: the next response.
Tell the patient to go over the whole past until every part of it is understood.
Tell the patient that the past cannot be changed, and so nothing can be done.
Tell the patient to forget the past, since only the future is of any use.
questions.e: The inheritance has three modes: the accumulated store, the hand dealt this life and what you are forming now. Only the third is yours, and that is where freedom lives: not in choosing the hand but in playing it. Agency is located in the next response, which is far lighter than fix your whole past.
questions.c: Locate agency in the next response, not the whole history

questions.q: “A deep cut becomes a pin-prick when practice raises the field the blow passes through, though the blow itself still comes.”
questions.e: Following the Holy Mother’s teaching in the lesson, practice does not cancel what ripens, but the field it passes through is raised, so what lands is radically attenuated. Agency is not out-muscling the past but allowing a higher source to transform the field the inheritance reaches you through.
questions.c: Practice raises the field, so the same blow lands far more lightly

questions.q: A man’s loop keeps coming back, and he wants a clean experiment. What does Conversation 4.5 suggest?
o: Fight the loop each time it fires, and count how often he manages to win.
Follow the loop each time it fires, to see where it leads and what it wants of him.
Let it run, neither feeding nor fighting it, and note whether it returns less fiercely.
Ignore the loop entirely, and judge the result only by how he feels in a month.
questions.e: Kai’s experiment is to neither push the loop away nor follow it, and to note over a week whether it returns slightly less fiercely. It tests whether starving a groove, rather than fighting it, shallows it.
questions.c: Neither feed nor fight the loop, and watch whether it weakens

questions.q: “Neuroscience supports one part of the picture: memory is stored in a spread-out way, like the grooves, which brings the two accounts closer.”
questions.e: Swamiji points to Pribram’s finding, offered as a bridge, that memory is stored holographically, spread through the whole brain like our loops. It shows the laboratory and contemplative accounts to be closer than they seem, though the two still diverge on where grooves finally reside.
questions.c: Spread-out storage is a bridge between the two accounts
